Lesson proper begins here

Anatomy & Physiology of the Eye

Structures, visual field, pathway, pupil, autonomic supply, and extraocular muscles.

pp. 1–2

Parts of the eye

StructureLecture description
CorneaMost anterior part where light passes through and is focused. Clear and dome-shaped.
IrisPigmented part of the eye. Color varies with nationality and melanin deposition.
PupilSmall aperture that dilates or constricts depending on focus and amount of light.
LensLocated behind the iris. Directs or condenses light onto the retina.
RetinaLight-sensitive thin film where images are projected. Its cell layers direct visual information toward the optic nerve.
Optic nerveCarries visual information to the brain for interpretation.
MaculaCenter of vision. Has the highest density of cones for clear vision.
Retinal vesselsMaintain the health and function of the eye.

Visual field

  • The entire area seen by the eye while looking at a central point.
  • Four quadrants: upper temporal, lower temporal, upper nasal, lower nasal.
  • The field extends farthest on the temporal sides.
  • Blind spot: lack of retinal receptors at the optic disc. Located 15 degrees temporal to the line of gaze.
  • Binocular vision: overlapping visual fields permit stereopsis or depth perception. Both eyes should work synchronously.

Visual pathway

Light→Cornea
main refracting surface→Pupil→Lens→Retina
sharpest at macula→Optic nerve→Optic chiasm→Optic tract→Lateral geniculate body→Optic radiation→Visual cortex
Must KnowNasal fibers decussate. Temporal fibers stay ipsilateral. After the chiasm, each side carries the opposite visual field from both eyes. Chiasmal lesions are associated with bitemporal defects. Post-chiasmal lesions are homonymous.

Pupillary reactions & autonomic supply

Light reaction

  • Direct: illuminated ipsilateral pupil constricts.
  • Consensual: contralateral non-illuminated pupil constricts.

Near reaction

  • Pupil constricts when shifting gaze from a far object to a near object.
  • Convergence: bilateral inward movement by the medial rectus muscles.
  • Accommodation: increased convexity of the lens due to ciliary muscle contraction.
  • Miosis is part of the reflex.

Autonomic supply

  • Parasympathetic: miosis.
  • Sympathetic: mydriasis and elevation of the upper eyelid through Müller’s muscle.

Extraocular muscles

Lecture MnemonicsLR6SO4 and LASOT. Lateral rectus is CN VI. Superior oblique is CN IV. Most other extraocular muscles are CN III.
MuscleNervePrimarySecondaryTertiary
Medial rectusCN IIIAdduction——
Lateral rectusCN VIAbduction——
Inferior rectusCN IIIDepressionExtorsionAdduction
Superior rectusCN IIIElevationIntorsionAdduction
Inferior obliqueCN IIIExtorsionElevationAbduction
Superior obliqueCN IVIntorsionDepressionAbduction
  • Rectus muscles are adductors except LR.
  • Oblique muscles are abductors.
  • Superior muscles are intorters.
  • Inferior muscles are extorters.

Cardinal gaze isolation

Up and outSuperior rectus
AbductionLateral rectus
Down and outInferior rectus
Up and inInferior oblique
AdductionMedial rectus
Down and inSuperior oblique

Example: looking upward right isolates the right superior rectus and left inferior oblique. Looking upper left isolates the left superior rectus and right inferior oblique.

History

Ocular History

Build rapport, define the complaint, then characterize symptoms systematically.

pp. 2–6

Components

  1. Chief complaint
  2. History of present illness
  3. Review of systems
  4. Past medical history
  5. Past ocular history
  6. Family history
  7. Social history
How to beginEstablish rapport. Introduce yourself. Make the patient comfortable before asking questions so information is easier to elicit.

Chief complaint & HPI

Chief complaint

  • Reason for consultation.
  • May be stated by a relative, companion, or guardian.
  • Rate reliability as good, fair, or poor.
  • List 1–2 symptoms or complaints with laterality and duration.

Lecture examples: “Right eye redness of 2 weeks duration” or “Eye redness of the left eye for 2 days duration.”

HPI

  • Get more detail on the chief complaint.
  • Begin with open-ended questions such as “How is your vision?”
  • Ask one question at a time. Do not overwhelm the patient.

Key symptom descriptors

ParameterLecture frameSample question
OnsetGradual or progressive“Unti-unti po bang nagsimula ang sintomas, o napapansin niyo pong palala nang palala?”
DurationAcute or chronic. Acute may be a few hours or days. Chronic may last a few months.“Biglaan po bang namula yung mata, o matagal na pong namumula yung mata niyo?”
FrequencyContinuous, intermittent, or episodic“Tuloy-tuloy po ba, pabugso-bugso, o may araw po ba na wala tapos meron?”
DegreeMild, moderate, or severe. Pain may be rated 1–10.“Gaano po kasakit yung mata niyo?”
LocationFocal or diffuse. Unilateral or bilateral.“Sa kanang mata, kaliwang mata, o pareho?”
ProgressionImproving, unchanged, or worsening.“Lumalala po ba ang sintomas habang tumatagal?”

Other questions to complete symptom elucidation

  • Treatment: Was treatment initiated? Did the patient self-medicate or consult another doctor?
  • Provoking and relieving factors: ask whether near or distance viewing changes symptoms, or whether measures such as a cold compress change discomfort.
  • Prior episodes: Is this the first time?
  • Associated signs and symptoms: ask what else accompanies the main complaint.

COLDERS

Common or concerning eye symptoms

Change in visionBlurred vision, loss of vision, floaters, flashing lights
Eye symptomsPain, redness, tearing
DiplopiaAsk whether it occurs in a specific gaze. The lecture links gaze-specific diplopia with a paretic or restricted muscle.

Past ocular & medical history

  • Ocular trauma and itchiness.
  • Spectacle prescription and use.
  • Previous vision status.
  • Systemic disease: diabetes, hypertension, thyroid problems, and other illnesses.
  • Prior eye surgery. Record eye, type of surgery, date, institution, doctor if possible, and outcome.

Family history

  • Hypertension, diabetes, cancer, and other neoplasms.
  • Glaucoma.
  • Myopia. The lecture states genetics is the highest risk factor.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa, color blindness, nyctalopia.
  • Retinoblastoma in younger patients ages 0–5.
  • ARMD and strabismus.
  • Congenital cataract warrants family history. Senile cataract does not because it is age related and common.

Social history

  • Tobacco: lecture links it with dry eyes and early cataract formation.
  • Alcohol and recreational drugs.
  • Occupation: ocular injury risk, office-work dry eye, protective goggles, and occupational hazards such as chemical exposure.
  • Hobbies: reading, computer use, or TV. Ask whether near or distant vision is used more.
  • The lecture mentions an emerging “weight loss injection” associated with eye problems.
History pattern recognition

Vision, Appearance & Ocular Sensation

Three symptom families taught in the lecture.

pp. 3–6

Vision changes and refractive patterns

Decline in visual acuity may arise from abnormalities along the optical and neurological pathway, including refractive error, ptosis, ocular media disturbance, retinal disease, optic nerve disease, or intracranial visual pathway abnormality.

PatternLecture cue
Difficulty with close workSuggestive of hyperopia or presbyopia. In the hyperopia illustration, the shorter eye focuses light behind the retina.
Difficulty with distanceSuggestive of myopia. The longer eye focuses light in front of the retina. The person moves nearer to see clearly.
EmmetropiaNormal vision, 20/20, no refractive error, with light rays converging at the retina.

Blurring of vision: two sorting frameworks

By laterality and painFirst identify unilateral vs bilateral. Then determine painful vs painless.
PainfulPainless
UnilateralHeadache, jaw pain, or claudication. Giant cell arteritis.Retinal causes: CRAO, retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage.
BilateralIntoxication, trauma, chemical or radiation exposures.Macular degeneration, cataract, glaucoma, vascular etiologies, stroke, or non-physiologic causes.
By onset and severityAsk whether sudden or gradual, then mild or severe.
MildSevere
SuddenDry eye syndromeCRAO
GradualRefractive errorCataract or glaucoma

Visual aberrations

AberrationPossible causes in lecture
Glare or photophobiaCorneal edema, cataract. Blurred and hazy image.
Visual distortionCentral serous chorioretinopathy or age-related macular degeneration.
Flashing or flickering lightsPosterior vitreous detachment or retinal detachment.
Floating spotsVitreous condensation. Common in myopic patients, especially high-grade cases.
OscillopsiaNystagmus.
DiplopiaStrabismus.
Nice to KnowNot all strabismic patients experience diplopia. Children born with strabismus may suppress the strabismic eye. Diplopia is described when strabismus occurs after visual maturation, including sudden onset or adulthood.

Red eye and color abnormalities

Differentiate redness arising from the lids and periocular area from redness of the globe.

  • Bacterial conjunctivitis: globe redness with mucopurulent discharge.
  • Nodular episcleritis: focal scleral redness with a red nodule.
  • Diffuse episcleritis: diffuse redness.
  • Subconjunctival hemorrhage: bright red bloodshot area. Lecture describes it as relatively benign and associated with trauma, pressure increases such as Valsalva or coughing or sneezing, or bleeding disorders.

Other color abnormalities

  • Jaundice: yellow sclera in liver problems.
  • Hyperpigmented lesion: ocular melanoma.
  • Bluish sclera: osteogenesis imperfecta or other severe connective tissue diseases.
  • White opacity or leukocoria: microbial keratitis or corneal infection.

Appearance abnormalities

FindingLecture description
PtosisDrooping eyelid. Pupil and corneal light reflex may be difficult to see because the upper lid covers the globe.
Focal growth or massGrowth on the lids or ocular surface. Examples include hordeolum and pinguecula.
ProptosisProtrusion of the eyeball due to a posterior pushing mechanism. The lecture uses exophthalmos specifically for thyroid eye disease.
Ocular misalignmentAssess corneal light reflex. Inward turning is esodeviation. Outward turning is exodeviation. Upward is hypertropia. Downward is hypotropia.
Abnormal sizeDisparity in corneal or globe size. Lecture examples include rhabdomyosarcoma, post-chemotherapy retinoblastoma with enophthalmos, and congenital glaucoma with buphthalmos.

Abnormalities in sensation

ComplaintLecture details
Periorbital painTenderness of lid, tear sac, sinuses, or temporal arteries.
Retro-orbital painOrbital inflammation, orbital myositis, optic neuritis. May be felt with eye movement.
Ocular painCorneal abrasion, corneal foreign body, glaucoma, corneal ulcer, or endophthalmitis.
Non-specific painOcular accommodation or binocular fusion.
Eye irritationItching, dryness, tearing, and secretions. Ropy or stringy discharge is linked with allergic conjunctivitis. Purulent discharge is linked with bacterial conjunctivitis. Crusting can occur with conjunctivitis.
HeadacheLecture sources include uncorrected refractive error and presbyopia, high or low blood pressure, and angle-closure glaucoma. Angle closure is described as intense unilateral eye pain and redness radiating to the head.
Ophthalmologic examination

Visual Acuity Determination

The lecture’s most emphasized first examination step.

pp. 6–9
Must KnowVisual acuity is the “vital signs” of the eye. Perform it before manipulation of the eye. This is especially important in trauma and medicolegal cases. p. 6

Distance visual acuity

  • Ability to identify objects or shapes at a given distance.
  • Use an age-appropriate or literacy-appropriate chart to avoid confusing literacy with visual impairment.
  • Distance VA is expressed as a fraction such as 20/20.
Numerator
distance at which test is performed/Denominator
distance at which a person with normal acuity can read that line

20/200: what the patient reads at 20 feet can be read by a person with normal acuity at 200 feet.

Recording line errors

  • Read left to right going down.
  • Record the number of letters correctly identified on each line.
  • For up to two errors on a line, add a minus notation such as 20/160 −2.
  • If the patient makes more than two mistakes on a line, use the line above and add the correctly read letters from the next line, up to +2. Lecture example: 20/60 +2.

Types of visual acuity charts

ChartLecture features
ETDRS or Bailey-LovieUsed for studies or research. More standardized, accurate, and reproducible. Equal number of letters, optotypes, spacing, and character size.
SnellenMost common. Characters and spacing vary by line. Usually tested at 20 ft or 6 m. Mirrors may extend distance in small rooms.
Tumbling EFor children or patients who are illiterate. Patient indicates the direction the fork faces.
Lea SymbolsStandard chart for children. Uses universal shapes without cultural or religious bias.

Snellen test: step-by-step

  1. Explain the procedure. Position the patient 20 ft or 6 m from a well-illuminated chart.
  2. Take uncorrected visual acuity first. If the patient wears glasses, the lecture instructs removal initially.
  3. Occlude one eye. Test one eye at a time. Make sure the occluder is not pressing the eye. Watch for peeking.
  4. Read from the largest line toward the smallest line that can still be read more than half correctly.
  5. Record the fraction using test distance as numerator and the last readable line as denominator.
  6. If VA is less than 20/20, recheck through a pinhole.
  7. If pinhole improves vision, the lecture says it is most likely an error of refraction. If not, explore other ocular pathology.
  8. Repeat on the opposite eye as applicable.

If the patient cannot read the largest letters

Reduce testing distance→Counting fingers→Hand movement→Light projection→Light perception
Reduce distanceMove closer in 5-foot increments. Example: reading the 20/200 line at 5 ft is recorded as 5/200.
Counting fingersBegin at 1 m or 3 ft. Move 1 ft closer if needed. Example: CF at 2 ft.
Hand movementAt 1 ft, determine whether horizontal or vertical hand motion can be detected. Avoid noisy jewelry.
Light projectionGood if all quadrants identified. Fair if 2–3. Poor if 1 of 4. Can record “+HM with good LP”.
Light perception+LP means presence of light is detected but direction is not. NLP means light is not detected.

Examination with glasses

If the patient uses glasses, proceed to examination with the current correction. If 20/20 is not achieved with current glasses, perform pinhole testing in each eye. Improvement with pinhole indicates a refractive error and the need for a new corrective prescription.

Near visual acuity

Red Exclamation Mark in LectureTesting distance: 14 inches or 35 cm. This is approximately half an arm’s length.
  • Use a Jaeger or near vision chart under good illumination.
  • If the patient normally wears reading glasses, wear them during testing.
  • Test one eye at a time.
  • Record the smallest correctly read figure and distance. Example: J2 at 14 inches or J2 at 35 cm.
  • If no standard near card is available, printed material or phone text may be used.

Standard recording abbreviations

Red Exclamation Mark in LectureKnow the standard abbreviations for ophthalmologic findings.
AbbreviationMeaningAbbreviationMeaning
VAVisual acuityODOculus dexter, right eye
OSOculus sinister, left eyeOUOculus uterque, both eyes
scWithout correctionccWith correction
phPinholeNVNear vision
Ophthalmologic examination

Visual Field Examination

Screening with confrontation, then pattern localization.

pp. 9–10

Confrontation visual field test

A screening method to identify abnormalities or lesions in the anterior and posterior visual pathways.

Humphrey Visual Field Test: computerized automated perimetry used for definitive evaluation. The lecture notes it is commonly required for PWD evaluation and used in glaucoma to assess and monitor visual-field impairment.

Static Wiggle Test

  1. Stand about one arm’s length away.
  2. Close one eye. Ask the patient to cover the opposite corresponding eye.
  3. Extend the arms about 2 ft apart, outside the patient’s visual field.
  4. Wiggle fingers while gradually moving toward the central field.
  5. Ask when movement is first seen or which finger is moving.
  6. Assess each quadrant, ideally each clock hour, one eye at a time.

Anterior vs posterior pathway defects

Anterior pathwayPosterior pathway
Glaucoma
Optic neuropathy
Optic neuritis
Compressive lesions		Stroke
Chiasmal tumors

Visual field defect patterns

DefectLecture localization or condition
Horizontal defectCentral retinal artery occlusion or ischemia of the optic nerve.
Blind right eyeRight optic nerve lesion or lesion of the eye itself.
Bitemporal hemianopsiaOptic chiasm lesion, including pituitary tumor. Crossing fibers are affected.
Left homonymous hemianopsiaRight optic tract lesion.
Homonymous left superior quadrantic defectPartial right optic radiation lesion in the temporal lobe. Only a portion of fibers may be involved.
Left homonymous hemianopsiaComplete interruption of fibers in the right optic radiation.
Ophthalmologic examination

External & Internal Eye Examination

Move from adnexa and alignment inward to pupils, sclera, conjunctiva, cornea, and lens.

pp. 10–11

External eye: what to examine

  • Eyebrows: fullness, hair distribution, and scaliness of underlying skin.
  • Position of the eye: inspect global protrusion from multiple angles.
  • Lids and palpebral fissure: height, asymmetry, redness, masses, pigmentation, lid margins, and lashes.
Red Exclamation Mark in LecturePosition of the eye or global protrusion: inspect from the front, right, left, and top.

Lid abnormalities

ConditionLecture description
PtosisDrooping upper eyelid. May result from old age, myasthenia gravis, oculomotor nerve damage, or Horner syndrome.
EntropionInward turning of lid margin. Lashes may turn inward and touch the globe.
EctropionLower lid turns outward. Conjunctiva may be exposed. If the punctum is exposed, tearing occurs. Lecture notes old-age laxity as a cause.
ExophthalmosProtrusion of the eyeball in thyroid eye disease.

Other lid conditions

Periorbital contusion hematomaTrauma can produce extensive bruising or hematoma. The eye may be difficult to see or close.
Capillary hemangiomaAbnormal vascular malformation of the eyelid that may almost cover the eye.
LymphangiomaMay be seen on lower-lid eversion. Enlarges during Valsalva.
Preseptal cellulitisSwollen, inflamed, erythematous, and red.

Pupils: inspection and light reaction

  • Inspect size, shape, and symmetry in dim light.
  • Inflammation such as uveitis may cause the iris to adhere to the lens and alter pupil shape during dilation.
  • Miosis: constriction. Mydriasis: dilation.
  • Anisocoria: difference in pupil size due to a defect in constriction or dilation of one pupil.
  • Simple anisocoria: pupil diameter difference ≥0.4 mm without known pathologic cause.

Swinging flashlight test

  • Swing light from one eye to the other with about a 1-second interval.
  • Normal: both pupils constrict.
  • Abnormal: dilation instead of constriction. The lecture links this with a relative afferent pupillary defect or Marcus Gunn pupil.

Near reaction

  • Test in dim and normal light because anisocoria may differ with lighting.
  • Hold a finger or pencil about 10 cm from the eye.
  • Ask the patient to alternate between the near target and a distant point behind it.
  • Observe miosis, convergence, and accommodation.

Direct and consensual reaction

  • Direct: ipsilateral constriction when that eye is illuminated.
  • Consensual: contralateral constriction in the opposite eye.

Conditions affecting the pupil

ConditionLecture description
Tonic or Adie pupilLarge, regular, usually unilateral. Light constriction is severely reduced, slowed, or absent. Near constriction is present but very slow.
CN III paralysisLarge fixed pupil to light and near effort, ptosis, and downward-outward eye deviation.
Horner syndromeSmall unilateral pupil with brisk light and near response but slow dilation, especially in dim light. Ipsilateral ptosis and often forehead anhidrosis.
Argyll Robertson pupilsSmall, irregular, usually bilateral. Normal near reaction. No light reaction.
Red Exclamation Mark in LectureHorner triad: Ptosis, Anhydrosis, Miosis. The lecture mnemonic is “P.A.M. is HORNY.”

Sclera and conjunctiva

Ask the patient to look up while depressing the lower lid to expose bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva. Inspect color and vascular patterns against the white sclera. Look for nodules or swelling. Ask the patient to look to each side and down.

ConditionKey distinction
PingueculaHarmless yellow triangular nodule in bulbar conjunctiva. Does not cross the cornea. If the triangular nodule crosses the cornea, it is a pterygium.
EpiscleritisBenign, usually painless, localized inflammation of episcleral vessels. Follows conjunctival movement.
Stye or hordeolumPainful, tender, red infection at inner or outer lid margin. Inner is linked to meibomian obstruction. Outer to eyelash follicle obstruction.
ChalazionSubacute, nontender, usually painless nodule from a blocked meibomian gland.

Cornea and lens

Use oblique lighting to inspect each cornea for opacities. Look through the pupil for lens opacities.

ConditionLecture appearance
Corneal arcusThin grayish-white arc or circle near the corneal edge. Often part of normal aging. Lecture notes it can also be seen with hyperlipoproteinemia.
Corneal scarSuperficial grayish-white corneal opacity secondary to old injury or inflammation. Shape and size vary with injury severity.
Kayser-Fleischer ringGolden to red-brown ring, sometimes green or blue. Copper deposition at the corneal periphery in Wilson disease.
PterygiumTriangular thickening of bulbar conjunctiva that grows across the cornea due to chronic UV exposure or irritation.
CataractWhitish opacity of the lens behind the pupil.
Ocular TraumaGet visual acuity first. Never palpate an eye with suspected open-globe injury because intraocular contents can extrude. p. 11
Ophthalmologic examination

Ocular Alignment & Motility

Corneal light reflex, six cardinal gazes, ductions, and versions.

pp. 11–12

Ocular alignment evaluation

  • Begin in primary position.
  • Observe the corneal light reflex.
  • A decentered reflex indicates ocular misalignment.
  • In the lecture example, a temporal corneal reflex accompanies inward eye deviation.
  • After correction, a central corneal reflex represents orthophoria or good alignment.
EsodeviationInward turning
ExodeviationOutward turning
HypertropiaUpward turning
HypotropiaDownward turning

Eye movement examination

  • Ask the patient to follow a finger, penlight, or small target through the six cardinal positions of gaze.
  • Move the target slowly.
  • Testing distance is 14 inches or 35 cm.
  • Fixation: 14 inches away at all cardinal gazes.
  • Ductions: monocular. Test one eye at a time.
  • Versions: binocular. Test both eyes.
  • Eyes only: avoid head movement. Tell the patient to keep the head steady.

Cardinal gazes and muscles tested

GazeMain muscles tested
RightRight lateral rectus + left medial rectus
Up-rightRight superior rectus + left inferior oblique
Down-rightRight inferior rectus + left superior oblique
LeftLeft lateral rectus + right medial rectus
Up-leftLeft superior rectus + right inferior oblique
Down-leftLeft inferior rectus + right superior oblique

Patient with exotropia

In the lecture image series, the patient follows the examiner’s finger. The first image is described as showing overactivity of the inferior oblique of both eyes when an imaginary line is drawn.

Ophthalmologic examination

Fundus Examination

Direct vs indirect ophthalmoscopy, ocular media, optic disc, vessels, and diabetic retinal findings.

pp. 12–14

How the fundus can be examined

  • Direct or indirect ophthalmoscopy.
  • Dilated or non-dilated.

Direct ophthalmoscope

  • Most common and readily available in clinics.
  • Limited view of the fundus.
  • Direct view.
  • Steps: dim lights, set focusing wheel to zero diopters, use right eye to examine right eye, position about 15 inches away at a 15° angle.

Indirect ophthalmoscope

  • Seen in ophthalmology clinics.
  • Wider fundus view.
  • Needs a condensing lens.
  • Image is reversed and inverted.

Ocular media: red-orange reflex

Red Flag in LectureAbsent red-orange reflex is explicitly labeled a red flag.

Optic disc evaluation

ConditionProcessAppearance
NormalTiny disc vessels give the disc its normal color.Yellowish orange to creamy pink. Tiny vessels emanate from the optic nerve. Margins are sharp.
PapilledemaElevated intracranial pressure causes intra-axonal edema along the optic nerve, leading to swelling.Swollen disc with blurred margins, loss of venous pulsations, and more numerous visible vessels.
GlaucomaIncreased intraocular pressure leads to increased deep cupping and atrophy.Pale. Cup is large and disc is thin.
Optic atrophyThe lecture describes enlargement of the physiologic cup beyond half the disc diameter.White or chalky white. Tiny disc vessels are absent.

Retinal vasculature

ConditionAppearance
Copper wiringArteries may become full and somewhat tortuous. Increased light reflex gives a bright coppery luster.
Silver wiringThe wall of a narrowed artery becomes opaque, with no visible blood.

Fundus in diabetes: findings listed in lecture

  • Soft exudates: fluffy and more superficial.
  • Hard exudates: deeper.
  • Dot hemorrhage.
  • Neovascularizations.
  • Vitreous hemorrhage.
  • Flame-shaped hemorrhage.
Lecture appendix

Visual Disability & PWD Card Appendix

Criteria and examples exactly within the scope of the lecture appendix.

pp. 9, 15

Visual disability criteria emphasized in the lecture

  • Vision 20/70 or worse in the better eye even with glasses, described in the lecture as Philippine NCDA criteria.
  • Visual field less than 20 degrees wide in the better eye.
  • Vision cannot be improved by eyeglasses, medication, or surgery.
  • The appendix similarly states best-corrected visual acuity in the better eye of 20/70 or 6/18 or worse, or a severely restricted field such as tunnel vision, with impairment not improved by standard treatment or refractive correction.
Do Not ConfuseThe lecture states that color blindness is not considered part of visual disability for this PWD qualification discussion.

Appendix classification

Generally eligible conditionsGenerally not eligible by themselves
Legal blindness
Low vision from retinal disease, including advanced diabetic retinopathy or retinitis pigmentosa
Advanced glaucoma with permanent visual-field loss
Advanced optic nerve disease such as optic atrophy
Permanent visual impairment from retinal detachment or macular degeneration
Severe corneal scarring not correctable with treatment
Other permanent visual impairments certified by an ophthalmologist		Myopia
Hyperopia
Astigmatism
Presbyopia
Simple strabismus
Wearing eyeglasses or contact lenses
Color blindness

These conditions alone usually do not qualify if vision can still be corrected.
Final tab

Cram Sheet

Rapid review of lecture-emphasized definitions, thresholds, patterns, sequences, and traps.

pp. 1–15

Pathway & field

  • Blind spot: 15° temporal to the line of gaze.
  • Visual pathway: cornea → pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve → chiasm → tract → LGB → optic radiation → occipital visual cortex.
  • Nasal fibers decussate. Temporal fibers remain ipsilateral.
  • Chiasm lesion: bitemporal defect.
  • Post-chiasmal lesion: homonymous defect.

EOM & pupil

  • LR6SO4 / LASOT.
  • Rectus muscles adduct except LR.
  • Obliques abduct.
  • Superior muscles intort. Inferior muscles extort.
  • Direct light reaction: ipsilateral constriction.
  • Consensual: contralateral constriction.
  • Near response: miosis + convergence + accommodation.

History anchors

  • Chief complaint: 1–2 symptoms, laterality + duration, and source reliability.
  • HPI: open-ended first. Ask one question at a time.
  • Common concerning symptoms: blurred or lost vision, floaters, flashing lights, eye pain, redness, tearing, diplopia.
  • Use lecture mnemonics COLDERS, LOFTSEA, CLITAA.

Refractive patterns & aberrations

  • Myopia: distance difficulty. Light focuses in front of retina.
  • Hyperopia: near difficulty. Light focuses behind retina in lecture diagram.
  • Emmetropia: 20/20 with light focused at retina.
  • Flashing lights: PVD or retinal detachment.
  • Floaters: vitreous condensation.
  • Oscillopsia: nystagmus.
  • Diplopia: strabismus.

Visual acuity sequence

VA first→Snellen at 20 ft / 6 m→If <20/20, pinhole→Reduce distance→CF→HM→LP
  • 20/200: patient reads at 20 ft what normal acuity reads at 200 ft.
  • ≤2 errors: use line with minus notation, e.g. 20/160 −2.
  • >2 errors: use previous line and add correctly read letters, up to +2.
  • Pinhole improvement → most likely refractive error.
Red Exclamation MarkNear visual acuity distance = 14 inches or 35 cm.
Red Exclamation MarkKnow: VA, OD, OS, OU, sc, cc, ph, NV.

Visual field test

  1. One arm’s length away.
  2. Cover corresponding eyes.
  3. Hands about 2 ft apart outside field.
  4. Wiggle toward central field.
  5. Patient reports first perception.
  6. Test all quadrants.

Field localization

  • Right optic nerve lesion → blind right eye.
  • Optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopsia.
  • Right optic tract → left homonymous hemianopsia.
  • Partial right temporal optic radiation → homonymous left superior quadrantic defect.
Red Exclamation MarkInspect eye position or global protrusion from front, right, left, and top.

Pupil differentiators

  • Adie: large, usually unilateral. Poor light reaction. Slow near response.
  • CN III palsy: large fixed pupil + ptosis + down-and-out eye.
  • Horner: small pupil + ptosis + anhidrosis. Slow dilation in dim light.
  • Argyll Robertson: small irregular pupils. Near response preserved. No light response.
Red Exclamation MarkHorner triad: Ptosis, Anhydrosis, Miosis. Lecture mnemonic: “P.A.M. is HORNY.”

Lid, conjunctiva, cornea

  • Pinguecula: does not cross cornea.
  • Pterygium: triangular tissue grows across cornea.
  • Hordeolum: painful, tender, red.
  • Chalazion: nontender, usually painless.
  • Kayser-Fleischer: peripheral copper deposition in Wilson disease.
  • Cataract: whitish lens opacity behind pupil.

Ocular motility

  • Target at 14 inches or 35 cm.
  • Ductions: monocular.
  • Versions: binocular.
  • Eyes move. Head stays steady.
  • Corneal light reflex off-center → misalignment.

Fundus rapid grid

FindingKey lecture cue
Direct ophthalmoscopyLimited direct view. Dim lights, zero diopters, right-to-right, 15 inches away at 15°.
Indirect ophthalmoscopyWider view. Condensing lens. Reversed and inverted image.
PapilledemaSwollen disc, blurred margins, loss of venous pulsations, more visible vessels.
GlaucomaDeep cupping and atrophy. Pale disc with large cup and thin disc.
Optic atrophyWhite or chalky white. Tiny disc vessels absent.
Copper wiringBright coppery luster.
Silver wiringOpaque narrowed arterial wall with no visible blood.

PWD appendix

  • Better-eye best-corrected VA 20/70 or 6/18 or worse, or severely restricted field such as tunnel vision.
  • Lecture criterion also states visual field <20° in the better eye.
  • Impairment cannot be improved by standard treatment or refractive correction.
  • Color blindness alone does not qualify in the lecture’s PWD discussion.
